title: One Bhagat a day
hook: a week of reading a different Bhagat each morning

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan: same raag, same refrain, same bow. Your line was all gurbani. Did you catch a name in a heading? Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

Seven sticky notes on the bathroom mirror. Each one has a name and a page number in marker: Ramanand. Bhikhan. Jaidev. Farid. A week of mornings, one voice per morning, before the phone gets a turn. It's the end of a week here too, so today does two jobs. It looks back at the voices of these seven days. And it hands over a small plan for the next seven: one Bhagat a day.
screen: `SEVEN NOTES ON A MIRROR.` → `ONE NAME EACH MORNING.` → `A WEEK BACK, A WEEK AHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the week behind us. Satta and Balvand, the minstrels whose Var, tradition says, was sung after a quarrel was forgiven. The saloks headed with Mardana's name, words to a friend. Sundar's Sadd, Guru Amar Das asking for singing, not weeping. The Gurus answering voices they would put differently, rather than erasing them. The trades of the Bhagats, reading like a whole street. And yesterday, all of it sung as gurbani. Now the week ahead. The Granth is long, and a reader can stand at the front of it and not know where to begin. So here's a doorway the size of a morning. The ang, the page number, is the address. Day one, Ramanand in Raag Basant, Ang 1195: a home colored with love. Day two, Bhikhan in Sorath, Ang 659: the Name as medicine. Day three, Jaidev in Gujri, Ang 526, the old poet. Day four, Farid in Asa, Ang 488: the heart and the lips. Day five, Parmanand and Surdas, side by side on Ang 1253. Day six, Ravidas in Gauri, Ang 345, the city without sorrow he calls Begampura. Day seven, a handful of Kabir's saloks, near the end of the book. Each reading is short. Some are a few lines. Read it slowly, once, in Gurmukhi if you can, in a translation if you can't. Then stop. The point isn't to cover ground. It's to sit with one voice long enough to hear how it speaks: Farid's longing, Kabir's sharp edge, Ravidas's dream of a city. Read one a day, and by the end of the week these names stop being a list and become people.
screen: `A WEEK OF VOICES, LOOKED BACK ON.` · `THE ANG IS THE ADDRESS.` · `SEVEN MORNINGS, SEVEN BHAGATS.` · `READ ONE SLOWLY, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `ONE A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a Bhagat today. If you can, open to one of those angs now, read a few lines slowly, and close it before the sit. If you can't, let the sit hold Ramanand's line in your own words: why go out looking, when home is colored with love. Breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. When a thought pulls you toward the day's to-do list, let the line call you back. The bell holds the time.
Ang. A page of the Guru Granth Sahib, the address for a week of mornings, one Bhagat read slowly on each one.
Your line: one a day. Tonight, write tomorrow's Bhagat and ang on a note and leave it where your morning starts. Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

screen: `DAY 798 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHICH VOICE SPEAKS TO YOU.`

howItsDone: Some Sikhs read from the Granth each day, and some keep a sehaj path, a slow reading of the whole Granth over time; a reader may also return to favorite shabads by their ang number.

match.prompt: the week ahead — tap the pairs.

myth: the point of one a day is to cover as much of the Granth as possible
the point is to sit with one voice long enough to hear how it speaks.

both are on Ang 1253, in Raag Sarang.

fork.setup: it's morning, the Granth is open to a Bhagat's hymn, and you have five minutes. what do you do?
options: read as many hymns as you can before time runs out.
read one hymn slowly, once, and stop.
save it for a free weekend.
fork.reveal: the plan is one voice a day, read slowly, so the names become people rather than a list.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ang, a page of the Guru Granth Sahib; also the word for a limb of the body.

trapdoor: what you thought: a reading plan.
what it means: one Bhagat each morning for a week, read slowly, so each voice becomes a person.
what a scholar hears: readers use the ang to find a hymn, the way an address finds a house, so a reading plan can be a list of names and angs.
recall: a bard, a poet of praise

sources.ref: Salok Kabir, near the end of the Granth
